hook.text: Why do people obey? Not just because of force. Most obedience comes from believing the authority is rightful.

buildup.text: Legitimacy is the belief that a political system or leader has the right to govern and command obedience.

discovery.text: It comes from tradition, divine sanction, law, popular consent, or personal charisma, depending on the culture.

twist.text: Legitimacy is fragile. When people stop believing in their leaders' right to rule, even powerful states can crumble.

climax.text: Every political system depends on legitimacy. Force alone can't sustain power. People must believe in the system.

punchline.text: Power without belief is just violence.

quiz.question: What is political legitimacy?
options: The amount of military force a leader has
The belief that a leader or system has the right to govern
Winning an election by majority vote

details.summary: Legitimacy is the belief among governed people that their rulers have the right to rule. Political systems survive through legitimacy rather than force alone, and legitimacy can derive from tradition, charisma, legal procedure, divine right, or performance.
details.whyItMatters: No political system survives on coercion alone. Understanding how legitimacy is constructed and maintained explains why some regimes endure for centuries while others collapse despite military strength.
takeaways: Legitimacy is the governed population's belief in rulers' right to rule
Political systems rely on legitimacy more than force for stability
Legitimacy derives from tradition, charisma, law, or performance

faq.question: How is legitimacy different from legality?
faq.answer: A government can be legal — following constitutional procedures — without being legitimate in the eyes of the people. Conversely, revolutionary governments may lack legal foundation but enjoy popular legitimacy. Legitimacy is about perceived moral right to rule, not legal formality.

faq.question: How do governments lose legitimacy?
faq.answer: Through corruption, economic failure, military defeat, broken promises, or visible disconnect between rulers' lives and citizens' suffering. Once legitimacy erodes, governments must rely increasingly on coercion, which further undermines legitimacy in a destabilizing cycle.
